title: A character-encoding 'best fit' manufactures a dash, and a dash turns a query string into a command line
index_line: T-0039 · EXEC · an encoding-conversion table maps an innocuous character to `-`; the interpreter reads it as an option · c/php · corroborated
invariant_violated: A component is assumed to be safe because its *own* parser rejects dangerous syntax, and because the dangerous characters are unrepresentable in the transport. Both assumptions die at the boundary: an encoding conversion with a 'best fit' table silently substitutes a near-enough character from the target character set, and the substituted character can be a leading dash. A payload assembled by a conversion table is syntax the sender never had to be able to type.

mechanism.does: the attacker sends a request whose parameters carry characters that will be re-encoded on their way to the interpreter
the platform's encoding conversion maps each character to its closest equivalent in the target codepage, so a soft hyphen becomes a plain hyphen
the re-encoded parameter is placed on the interpreter's command line, exactly as the platform is documented to do for CGI execution
the interpreter's own argument parser sees a leading dash and treats the value as an option instead of data
an allowed option enables code execution or file write, so the 'data' argument becomes a directive
the interpreter executes the attacker-supplied code in the web server's context

source.http.request.value: the query string: an encoded character the sender cannot type, followed by an option name and its value

sink.exec.noshell.value: the CGI interpreter invocation whose argv is assembled from the request — argument injection into the interpreter itself

encoding.url.value: percent-encoded multibyte and 0xAD-class characters chosen for what the conversion maps them to

guard.none.value: no separation between options and data, and no check that the re-encoded value cannot begin an option

preconditions.expr: the deployment runs the interpreter as a CGI on a platform whose encoding conversion has a best-fit table (Windows with non-UTF-8 codepages)
the CGI path forwards the query string as command-line arguments (the documented behaviour a mitigation has to disable)
the server is reachable and passes the request to CGI rather than to a module

check.spec: request a path that the CGI mapping handles and confirm the interpreter's argv receives the decoded parameters (a probe that echoes its own argv)

success: a request that contains no ASCII dash still causes an option to be parsed — the dash came from the conversion
the interpreter executes an option such as a source-file or auto-prepend primitive and returns output
the same request is inert when the platform runs the interpreter as a server module or on a UTF-8-only codepage
failure_like: the conversion table is strict and drops unmappable characters instead of substituting
the deployment puts `--` between options and the request-derived values
false_positive: a payload using a literal `-` that the application sanitised — then the bug is the sanitiser, not the encoding
an error from the interpreter naming the option: it parsed the dash, which is the precondition, but check whether the option was *useful*

hazards: the same class exists wherever an encoding conversion sits between the input and a parser: codepage best-fit, Unicode normalisation (fullwidth dash/solidus), and legacy charset transcoding
the CWE published for this is 'argument injection' and the mitigation is an option separator — the conversion table is a platform fact you cannot patch away
probes must not contain the character they are testing for; the payload has to arrive as multi-byte text and become the metacharacter in transit
related but distinct from T-0022: there the interpreter is *given* the query string by design; here the platform's conversion creates the syntax
non_transfers: platforms whose conversion is strict (no best-fit substitution)
interpreter invocations that insert an option terminator before request-derived values
